extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of fantasy, and aspiring fantasy writers interested in worldbuilding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for creating and using magic systems in fantasy fiction — includes Sanderson's Laws of Magic and the hard-vs-soft magic distinction to guide how magic is explained, limited, and used to resolve conflict in stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's First Law
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's ability to solve conflict with magic is directly proportional to how well the reader understands said magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law advises that if you want to use magic to resolve plot conflicts, the mechanics of that magic must be sufficiently explained to the reader; otherwise using magic as a deus ex machina will feel unsatisfying. (Verbatim wording from the article.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Second Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses, limits and costs are more interesting than powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on giving magic clear limitations, costs, or drawbacks rather than only impressive abilities — these constraints create narrative interest, stakes, and opportunities for character and plot development. (Verbatim wording from the article.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Third Law
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should expand on what is already a part of the magic system before something entirely new is added, as this may otherwise entirely change how the magic system fits into the fictional world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing or escalating a magic system, build out from established elements rather than introducing wholly new mechanics mid-story; sudden additions can undermine internal consistency and worldbuilding. (Verbatim/paraphrase from the article.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Zeroth Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Always err on the side of what's awesome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A meta-guideline prioritizing entertainment and imaginative payoff — when in doubt about a creative choice in a magic system, favor what will be exciting or memorable for the reader. (Verbatim wording from the article.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard magic system characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard magic systems follow specific rules; the magic is controlled and explained to the reader in the narrative detailing the mechanics behind the way the magic 'works' and can be used for building settings that revolve around the magic system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hard system when you want the magic to drive plot mechanics, problem-solving, and logical consequences. Provide explicit rules and workings so readers understand what can and cannot be done; this supports using magic to resolve conflicts in believable ways. (Description taken from the article explaining hard magic.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft magic system characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft magic systems may not have clearly defined rules or limitations, or they may provide limited exposition regarding their workings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft magic is best when the goal is to create a sense of wonder or mystery. Because the mechanics are not fully explained, soft magic should typically not be relied on to solve tightly plotted problems without risking a feeling of arbitrariness. (Description and implication drawn from the article's explanation of soft magic.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing hard vs soft magic (usage guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both terms are approximate ways of characterizing two ends of a spectrum; hard magic is used for settings that revolve around the magic system, while soft magic is used to create a sense of wonder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which style matches your story's needs: choose hard magic when you want rules-based problem solving and plot-driven uses of magic; choose soft magic when atmosphere, mystery, and awe are primary. The page frames these as ends of a spectrum rather than strict categories. (Synthesis of the article's discussion.)
